etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *bayt- (“house”). Cognate with Akkadian bītum, Arabic بَيْت (bayt) and Amharic ቤት (bet).

funFacts: The letter ב (bet) is named after this word, and Greek beta comes from the same Phoenician letter name.
Arabic بَيْت (bayt) also means a line of verse — Turkish beyit “couplet” comes from it — and Hebrew בַּיִת is a stanza too.
Bethlehem is בֵּית לֶחֶם, “house of bread”.
pitfalls: The plural is irregular: בַּיִת → בָּתִּים.
In compounds the first word changes to בֵּית־: בֵּית סֵפֶר “school”, בֵּית חוֹלִים “hospital”.
subtleties: בַּבַּיִת is “at home”; “(to) home” with motion is הַבַּיְתָה: אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ הַבַּיְתָה.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *dalt- (“door”), cognate with Akkadian daltum, Ugaritic dlt and Aramaic דַּלְתָּא. The -t, once the feminine ending, was reinterpreted as part of the root; the noun took the segolate shape. Doublet of the letter name דָּלֶ״ת.

funFacts: The letter ד (dalet) is named after the door, and Greek delta Δ comes from the same Phoenician letter.
pitfalls: דֶּלֶת is feminine although it does not end in -ָה: הַדֶּלֶת הַזֹּאת, הַדֶּלֶת פְּתוּחָה.
Plural דְּלָתוֹת; the dual דְּלָתַיִם is “a double door”.
subtleties: The -et ending is an old feminine -t (Wiktionary) — the reason the word is feminine.

The article is הָ before א: הָאָרוֹן; “in the cupboard” is בָּאָרוֹן.
subtleties: Context decides between a wardrobe, a coffin and the holy Ark — all are boxes that keep something.

funFacts: Arabic كَأْس (kaʾs) “glass, cup” is the same old Semitic word.
The “cup of salvation” of Psalm 116 is כּוֹס יְשׁוּעוֹת.
pitfalls: Standard Hebrew treats כּוֹס as feminine without a feminine ending: כּוֹס אַחַת, הַכּוֹס הַזֹּאת, הִיא. Wiktionary also records masculine use, common in speech.
Write it with its vowel or in a clear context: unvocalized כוס can also be read as a vulgar slang word (Wiktionary lists it).
subtleties: כּוֹס is both “glass” and “cup”: כּוֹס מַיִם “a glass of water”, כּוֹס קָפֶה “a cup of coffee”.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

meaningForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Meals at the table — and the washing-up after.

examples.tr: The plate is empty.
The plates are in the cupboard.
I’m washing the plates.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic, akin to Arabic صَحْن (ṣaḥn, “bowl, plate”) and Ge’ez ṣaḥl (“bowl, jar, pan”).

funFacts: Arabic صَحْن (ṣaḥn) is a relative; Turkish sahan, the little pan of sahanda yumurta, comes from the Arabic.
pitfalls: Feminine (the -ַת ending): הַצַּלַּחַת הַזֹּאת, הִיא.
The plural is צַלָּחוֹת (the second vowel changes to qamats).
subtleties: A “flying saucer” is a צַלַּחַת מְעוֹפֶפֶת — literally a flying plate.
